source_text: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ παρ’ Ἑβραίων τὰ τῶν φιλοσόφων ἐσκευωρῆσθαι δόγματα μικρὸν ὕστερον διαληψόμεθα, πρότερον δέ, ὅπερ ἀκόλουθον ἦν, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωυσέα χρόνων ἤδη λεκτέον, δἰ ὧν δειχθήσεται ἀναμφηρίστως πάσης σοφίας ἀρχαιοτάτη ἡ κατὰ Ἑβραίους φιλοσοφία. εἴρηται μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων ἀκριβῶς Τατιανῷ ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἕλληνας, εἴρηται δὲ καὶ Κασσιανῷ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν· ἀπαιτεῖ δὲ ὅμως τὸ ὑπόμνημα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιδραμεῖν τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον εἰρημένα. Ἀπίων τοίνυν ὁ γραμματικός, ὁ Πλειστονίκης ἐπικληθείς, ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ τῶν Αἰγυπτιακῶν ἱστοριῶν, καίτοι φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος, ἅτε Αἰγύπτιος τὸ γένος, ὡς καὶ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων συντάξασθαι βιβλίον, Ἀμώσιος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως μεμνημένος καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὸν πράξεων, μάρτυρα παρατίθεται Πτολεμαῖον τὸν Μενδήσιον. καὶ τὰ τῆς λέξεως αὐτοῦ ὧδε ἔχει· κατέσκαψε δὲ τὴν Ἀουαρίαν Ἄμωσις κατὰ τὸν Ἀργεῖον γενόμενος Ἴναχον, ὡς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις ἀνέγραφεν ὁ Μενδήσιος Πτολεμαῖος. ὁ δὲ Πτολεμαῖος οὗτος ἱερεὺς μὲν ἦν, τὰς δὲ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέων πράξεις ἐν τρισὶν ὅλαις ἐκθέμενος βίβλοις κατὰ Ἄμωσίν φησιν Αἰγύπτου βασιλέα Μωυσέως ἡγουμένου γεγονέναι Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου πορείαν, ἐξ ὧν συνῶπται κατὰ Ἴναχον ἠκμακέναι τὸν Μωσέα. παλαίτατα δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τὰ Ἀργολικά, τὰ ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου λέγω, ὡς Διονύσιος ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις διδάσκει, τούτων δὲ † τεσσαράκοντα μὲν γενεαῖς νεώτερα τὰ Ἀττικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Κέκροπος τοῦ διφυοῦς δὴ καὶ αὐτόχθονος, ὥς φησι κατὰ λέξιν ὁ Τατιανός, ἐννέα δὲ τὰ Ἀρκαδικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Πελασγοῦ· λέγεται δὲ καὶ οὗτος αὐτόχθων. τούτων δὲ ἄλλαιν δυοῖν νεώτερα τὰ Φθιωτικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Δευκαλίωνος. εἰς δὲ τὸν χρόνον τῶν Τρωϊκῶν ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου γενεαὶ μὲν εἴκοσι ἢ μιᾷ πλείους διαριθμοῦνται, ἔτη δέ, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, τετρακόσια καὶ πρόσω. εἰ δὲ τὰ Ἀσσυρίων πολλοῖς ἔτεσι πρεσβύτερα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἀφ’ ὧν Κτησίας λέγει, φανήσεται τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ ἔτει τῆς Ἀσσυρίων ἀρχῆς, τῆς δὲ Βηλούχου τοῦ ὀγδόου δυναστείας τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ ἡ Μωυσέως κατὰ Ἄμωσιν τὸν Αἰγύπτιον καὶ κατὰ Ἴναχον τὸν Ἀργεῖον ἐξ Αἰγύπτου κίνησις. ἦν δὲ κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα κατὰ μὲν Φορωνέα τὸν μετὰ Ἴναχον ὁ ἐπὶ Ὠγύγου κατακλυσμὸς καὶ ἡ ἐν Σικυῶνι βασιλεία, πρώτου μὲν Αἰγιαλέως, εἶτα Εὔρωπος, εἶτα Τελχῖνος, καὶ ἡ Κρητὸς ἐν Κρήτῃ. Ἀκουσίλαος γὰρ Φορωνέα πρῶτον ἄνθρωπον γενέσθαι λέγει· ὅθεν καὶ ὁ τῆς Φορωνίδος ποιητὴς εἶναι αὐτὸν ἔφη πατέρα θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἐντεῦθεν ὁ Πλάτων ἐν Τιμαίῳ κατακολουθήσας Ἀκουσιλάῳ γράφει·
pass_a_gloss: We will discuss a little later how the doctrines of the philosophers were seen among the Hebrews, but first, as was fitting, we must speak about the times of Moses, through which it will be shown clearly that the Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has spoken precisely about these things in his work Against the Greeks, and also Cassian has spoken about them in the first of his Exegetical works; however, our memorandum also demands that we run through the things said according to the place. Apion the grammarian, also called Plistonicus, in the fourth of his Egyptian histories, although he is hostile towards the Hebrews, as an Egyptian by birth, and has even written a book against the Jews, mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events that occurred during his reign, and presents Ptolemy of Mendes as a witness. And his words are as follows: Amosis, who became king after Argive Inachus, destroyed Auaris, as Ptolemy of Mendes wrote in his Chronicles. This Ptolemy was a priest who, in three whole books, set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings, and he says that, under Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews, led by Moses, made their journey out of Egypt, from which it is clear that Moses flourished during the time of Inachus. The most ancient of the Greek things, however, are the Argolic things, which I call the things from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles. These, then, are forty generations older than the Attic things, which are from Cecrops, who was, as Tatian says word for word, a double-born and autochthonous man. The Arcadic things, which are from Pelasgus, are nine generations older; and this Pelasgus is also said to be autochthonous. The Phthiotic things, which are from Deucalion, are younger than these by two generations. As for the time of the Trojan War, twenty generations or a little more are counted from Inachus, and, so to speak, four hundred years. But if the Assyrian things are, as Ctesias says, many years older than the Greek things, it will be shown that in the second and four hundredth year of the Assyrian reign, and in the second and thirtieth year of the eighth dynasty of Belochus, the departure of Moses from Egypt, under Amosis the Egyptian and Inachus the Argive, took place. Now, in Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who came after Inachus, there was the flood that occurred in the time of Ogygus, and the kingdom in Sicyon, first of Aegialeus, then of Eurypus, then of Telchin, and the kingdom of Crete in Crete. For Acusilaus says that Phoroneus was the first man to be born; hence, the poet of the Phoroneis says that he was the father of mortal men. From this, Plato, following Acusilaus, writes in the Timaeus:
pass_b_english: We will address a little later how the philosophers' doctrines were received among the Hebrews, but first, as proper order requires, we must speak of the times of Moses; through them it will be shown beyond dispute that the philosophy of the Hebrews is the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has treated these matters exactly in his work Against the Greeks, and Cassian has done so in the first of his Exegetical books; nevertheless our memorandum also demands that we run through the statements relevant to this place. Apion the grammarian, surnamed Plistonicus, in the fourth book of his Egyptian Histories — though he is hostile toward the Hebrews, being an Egyptian by birth, and has even composed a book against the Jews — mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events of his reign, and produces Ptolemy of Mendes as a witness. His words run thus: Amosis, who became king after the Argive Inachus, destroyed Avaris, as Ptolemy of Mendes recorded in his Chronicles. This Ptolemy was a priest who set out the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three whole books, and he says that under Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews, led by Moses, made their exodus from Egypt, from which it follows that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus. The most ancient of Greek traditions are the Argolic ones, that is, those reckoned from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles. These are forty generations older than the Attic traditions, which begin with Cecrops, whom Tatian quotes verbatim as a double-born and autochthonous man. The Arcadian traditions, which begin with Pelasgus, are nine generations older, and Pelasgus is also said to be autochthonous. The Phthiotic traditions, which begin with Deucalion, are younger than these by two generations. Concerning the time of the Trojan War, twenty generations or a little more are counted from Inachus, and, so to speak, four hundred years. But if the Assyrian traditions are, as Ctesias says, many years older than the Greek ones, it will appear that in the four hundred and second year of the Assyrian empire, and in the thirty-second year of the eighth dynasty of Belochus, the departure of Moses from Egypt took place under Amosis the Egyptian and Inachus the Argive. In Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who came after Inachus, there occurred the flood of Ogygus, and the kingdom in Sicyon — first of Aegialeus, then of Europs, then of Telchin — and the kingdom of Crete in Crete. review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex chronological arguments and historical references. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek text. The translation of 'ἀναμφηρίστως' as 'clearly' (A) and 'beyond dispute' (B) is acceptable within the bounds of fluency. The specific years (402nd and 32nd) match the Greek 'δευτέρῳ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ' and 'δευτέρῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ'.
